newsitem.title: UK: Catholics say "Orangemen" thwarting march talks.
newsitem.headline: Catholics say "Orangemen" thwarting march talks.

text.p: Roman Catholics in a Northern Ireland sectarian flashpoint accused the powerful Protestant Orange Order on Monday of blocking mediation aimed at easing fears over a contentious "Orange" pro-British parade.
In a statement, Orange Order head Robert Saulters declared tersely that he would not discuss the march, planned for July at Drumcree near Portadown town, with Irish republican hardliners.
Catholic nationalist residents said they had wanted to send a delegation, which will soon meet Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, to talks with Saulters and his colleagues.
"We are committed to finding a just and lasting resolution to the parades issue in Portadown," the Catholic Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition said in a statement.
"Local people just do not understand why the Orange Order will not allow this to happen."
With mediation hopes shrouded in confusion, Nobel peace prize nominee John Hume, who launched the initiative on Sunday night, said he had announced it after consulting Saulters.

"Given that I want to do whatever I can...to help avoid a repeat of last year's events, I will be endeavouring to clarify the situation. Therefore I hope it's not the end of the process," Hume, who leads the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, told BBC radio.
Last July the British province was engulfed in street clashes when police tried to stop the parade.
Hume's overnight statement had raised hopes of an early end to annual province-wide tension over Orange Order parades, which the Catholic minority regards as anti-Irish.
He had said he would soon convene a landmark meeting between Saulters and residents in Portadown's Garvaghy Road who object to "Orangemen" parading past their homes.
However, Saulters said that there had been "some misunderstanding" following Hume's press statement on Sunday.
He insisted he would abide by his organisation's long-standing opposition to talks with anyone linked to the outlawed Irish Republican Army or its Sinn Fein political arm.
"In keeping with the policy of Grand Lodge, I will not be meeting with anyone who has any connection with IRA/Sinn Fein," Saulters said in a two-sentence statement.

In the past, "Orangemen" have refused to hold talks with Breandan MacCionnaith, a leader of the Garvaghy residents, because he was jailed for four years in 1981 for an arms offence and hijacking a vehicle.
MacCionnaith denies links with the IRA, which has waged a 28-year guerrilla campaign against British rule, or Sinn Fein.

The order's Grand Lodge controlling body said in a separate statement that the IRA and Sinn Fein had manipulated certain resident groups into whipping up opposition aimed at preventing Orange marches that have been held for generations.
